final_message:
0.399323, so this is a gain of 1.73e-4. The law is in the refine lane.

| Item | Result |
|---|---|
| Law | 128 atoms: nested ladders split (99, 22, 5, 1), plus an atom at 0 |
| Certified value | 0.399496 (the float optimum is 0.3994957) |
| Strategy time | 2.5 s |
| Certification time here | 53 s wall, about 40 s CPU, with load average 49 on 12 cores |
| `confidence` / `report.json` | 0.001, because the value is 1.2e-3 below the 0.400695 limit |

**Timeout risk:** on this machine, certification takes much longer than the 20 s limit. The parent's 112-atom law took 42 s wall here and was still certified. The lane note also says the grader certifies 128 atoms in a few seconds. But if the grader is as slow as this machine, the run will time out and score zero on this instance. To go back to the parent's cost, set `LADDER_ATOMS = 112` in `strategy.py`.

**Why I stopped:**
- The value depends only on the lexicographic order of the atoms. The optimiser gave zero weight to all extra atoms I tried: 1/4, 1/3, 3/8, 5/8, 2/3, 1/8, 1/16, and points between the scales. Changing the scale gap (1 to 4) did not change the value.
- At 128 atoms, (99, 22, 5, 1) was the best of the ten 3-, 4- and 5-scale splits I tried.
- Almost all partial sums are distinct, so certification costs about K⁴/6 dictionary operations. Smaller integer weights did not make it faster. Thus the only remaining way to gain value is more atoms, and the time limit stops that.

No law found here reaches the 0.400695 limit.
